title: Quantized Token-Budget Scheduler — exploratory notes
content:
Purpose and motivation:

This note explores an alternative admission and scheduling approach that treats per-request resource consumption primarily as token budgets rather than raw concurrency or GPU-slot counts. The intuition: latency-sensitive workloads often differ in token demand distribution between prefix and generation phases. Quantizing budgets into discrete slot classes (tiny, small, medium, large) can simplify admission and make bandwidth reclamation faster, while allowing finer-grained KV-cache and kernel hints for efficient execution.

Goals:
- Provide predictable latency SLOs for tenants with mixed request types (short prompts + long generations).
- Enable soft isolation by allocating token budgets rather than hard slot counts.
- Reduce tail latencies caused by KV cache thrashing when many variable-length requests interleave.
- Allow fast rebalancing under bursty arrivals without global coordination.

Basic idea (high level):
- Each tenant T has a replenishing quarterly-style token budget bucket B_T measured in "token-units". Token-units are consumed at admission time based on a cheap estimator of expected token usage (prefix + expected generation).
- Instead of continuous budgets, we quantize possible admission sizes into {Q0=8u, Q1=32u, Q2=128u, Q3=512u} where u is a unit (1 token-unit approximates 1 model token). Each admission picks the smallest Qi >= estimated tokens.
- The scheduler maintains per-GPU slot pools for each Qi class. A Qi slot corresponds to a reservation sized to execute requests in that quant class with pre-allocated KV-cache window and kernel selection hints (e.g., block sizes, attention kernel lanes).
- If no Qi slot is available for a tenant, the admission controller attempts (in order): 1) borrow from a larger Qi+1 pool if the tenant has available budget, 2) perform a lightweight hedged admission (provision temporary micro-slot with higher eviction probability), 3) reject/queue based on tenant priority and deadline.

Why quantize?
- Simpler accounting: rounding up to discrete buckets reduces churn in budgeting and makes pre-sizing of KV frames easier.
- Kernel and memory planning: each class can be mapped to a tuned kernel path and KV allocation strategy (e.g., Q0 uses minimal KV prefetch, Q3 uses large KV reserve).
- Faster reclaim: micro-slots can be preempted more easily when you know the class guarantees.

KV-cache awareness:
- Admission records a KV-hint: prefix-length, expected generation window, and an affinity tag derived from recent cache keys (hash of top-k prefix tokens).
- Scheduler co-locates similar affinity admissions onto same worker within a short time window to increase KV hit-rate. Affinity is best-effort and decays after N seconds to avoid long-term imbalance.
- When a Qi slot is preempted, we try to evict only non-affine entries first; eviction strategy favors cheap-to-recompute KV shards (e.g., tokenized prefix-only entries) and preserves long-lived cached decoder state for high-value tenants.

Admission algorithm (sketch):
1) Request arrives with metadata {tenant, max_deadline_ms, prompt_tokens, expected_gen_tokens_hint}.
2) Compute est_tokens = prompt_tokens + gen_hint (default conservative multiplier if missing).
3) Choose quant class Qi = min Qi s.t. Qi >= est_tokens.
4) Check tenant budget: budget_ok = B_T >= Qi. If not, soft-fail fast: offer two alternatives (degraded mode with cap at Q smaller class if available, or queue with ETA).
5) Try fast path: allocate a free Qi slot on any compatible worker that has affinity for tenant or matching KV-hint. If found, deduct Qi from B_T and accept.
6) If none free, try borrow policy: find next larger Qj (j>i) with free slot and B_T >= Qj; if found, accept but mark request as "overprovisioned" and attach eviction priority low.
7) If still none, attempt micro-slot admission: allocate micro-CPU-only admission that starts light compute and triggers early prefetch of KV. Micro-slot is allowed only for requests with high deadline slack and is cancellable.
8) Final fallback: place into per-tenant queue ordered by (deadline,priority,est_tokens) with a capped queue depth.

Budget replenishment and fairness:
- Each tenant bucket B_T replenishes at a configured rate R_T (tokens/sec) derived from their SLA/commit. Unused tokens decay slowly to allow short bursts.
- To enforce fairness between noisy neighbors, we maintain a dynamic smoothing window W (e.g., 60s) and reduce transient borrow capacity if a tenant consumes > alpha * R_T in that window.
- Emergency throttle: a global governor reduces per-tenant effective R_T when cluster-level token consumption exceeds a threshold; this preserves headroom for low-latency classes.

Timeouts, cancellations, and hedging:
- Timeouts are handled by two layers: admission latency budget (time to start) and execution deadline (generation completion). If start latency > start_deadline, scheduler can either preempt a lower-priority micro-slot or return an early-reject to client.
- Hedging: for very latency-sensitive small requests (Q0/Q1) we adopt speculative hedging: dispatch to two different workers if estimated start time > hedging_threshold. Hedged requests incur budget consumption on only the winner; the loser’s budget is credited back partially (charged for wasted prefetch cost).

Kernel and runtime hooks:
- Each Qi class maps to kernel tuning presets (tensor layout, block size, fused attention path, quantized GEMM kernels). Admission controller passes class id and affinity tag to worker; worker uses this to warm-up specialized kernels and pre-allocate KV buffer of size proportional to Qi.
- Workers expose fast rejects when KV pressure surpasses a class-specific threshold; admission controller can downgrade admitted requests to smaller Qi at runtime with customer-visible signals (e.g., "approximate mode: shorter gen") for best-effort QoS.

Operational metrics to track (prototype):
- per-tenant token consumption rate, bucket fill level, and peak bursts
- Qi slot utilization per worker and per-GPU
- KV hit-rate conditioned on affinity co-location window
- micro-slot eviction frequency and average reclaimed tokens
- request start latency distribution per Qi class and per-tenant
- number of hedged requests and partial credit applied

Open questions / trade-offs:
- Estimation accuracy: worst-case misestimates may under-provision (leading to mid-run rejection) or over-provision (wasteful token drain). Should we use light-weight ML estimator vs heuristics?
- Billing semantics: if we quantize and overprovision, what is fair billing? Bill by actual tokens consumed, but enforce rate limits by Qi reservation? Need clear customer-facing documentation.
- Complexity vs benefit: this design adds per-class slot bookkeeping, worker affinity logic, and micro-slot paths. Need cost/benefit analysis vs simpler per-request token bucketing without quantization.
- KV affinity fairness: aggressive affinity boosts KV-hit but can create hotspots. We need decay policies and fallback redistribution.

Prototype plan (next steps):
1) Implement a simulation that replays production trace (last 7 days) using quantized bucket rules and measure start latency, KV-hit, and wasted tokens.
2) Add a lightweight estimator: median-based generation-size prior per tenant + a short ML fallback for unknown tenants.
3) Wire minimal worker-side Qi preset: pre-allocated KV buffer sizes and one alternate kernel path for Q0 vs Q3.
4) Run an A/B against current admission controller on a small fleet; measure tail-latency and cost per token.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is exploratory and intentionally aggressive on per-tenant budgeting semantics. Looking for feedback on quantization levels, replenishment rates, and whether micro-slots introduce unacceptable oscillations.
- If you have traces to share (especially long-tail generation jobs) please tag them in INF-5321 so the simulator can exercise extremes.

Quick sketch pseudocode (very rough):
accept(request):
  est = estimate_tokens(request)
  q = quantize(est)
  if bucket[tenant] < q:
    if allow_downgrade and bucket[tenant] >= smaller_q: offer downgrade
    else return soft_reject
  slot = find_free_slot(q, affinity=request.affinity)
  if slot: allocate(slot); bucket[tenant] -= q; return accept
  slot = find_borrow_slot(q)
  if slot: allocate(slot, overprovision=true); bucket[tenant] -= slot.q; return accept
  if can_micro_admit(request): micro_allocate(request); return pending
  enqueue_per_tenant(request); return queued

End of note.

[unresolved] tied topics: billing impact, multi-tenant hot-swap policies, integration with autoscaler and dedicated pools.
summary: Exploratory draft for a quantized token-budget based scheduler that uses discrete token classes, KV affinity, micro-slots, and hedging to improve latency guarantees and KV-hit rates while enabling budgeted per-tenant control. Includes algorithm sketches, open questions, and a prototype plan.
